# Review: `diff.patch` before/after scope (PR 865 snapshot)

> Produced from the VOSTD coding-guideline review criteria and the skill's API-contract criteria.
> Scope: the complete `diff.patch`, with `before/` and `after/` used only for surrounding source context.

**Bottom line:** The patch blocks LoongArch from compiling: it comments out most of the architecture module declarations and all of the architecture entry points while shared code still calls those items on LoongArch. Restore this executable architecture surface before merging; the verification additions can remain scoped to the page-table code without deleting unrelated runtime code.

## High

### The patch removes the LoongArch runtime architecture surface

- **Guideline:** `preserve-exec-code`
- **Location:** `ostd/src/arch/loongarch/mod.rs:3`
- **Evidence:** The before version declares `pub mod boot;`, `pub(crate) mod cpu;`, `pub mod device;`, `pub(crate) mod iommu;`, `pub mod kernel;`, `pub(crate) mod pci;`, `pub mod qemu;`, `pub(crate) mod serial;`, `pub(crate) mod task;`, and `pub mod trap;`, and defines `late_init_on_bsp`, `init_on_ap`, `interrupts_ack`, `tsc_freq`, `read_tsc`, `read_random`, and `enable_cpu_features`. The after version wraps those declarations and every one of those functions in block comments (`ostd/src/arch/loongarch/mod.rs:3-7`, `:9`, `:11-14`, and `:16-69`). These are not dead declarations: shared source still calls `arch::enable_cpu_features()` and `arch::late_init_on_bsp()` (`ostd/src/lib.rs:87,124`), imports/calls `arch::serial` (`ostd/src/lib.rs:96-99`), calls `crate::arch::trap::init()` and `crate::arch::init_on_ap()` (`ostd/src/boot/smp.rs:133,137`), and calls `crate::arch::interrupts_ack(...)` (`ostd/src/trap/handler.rs:66`).
- **Problem:** On a LoongArch build those selected architecture items no longer exist, so name resolution fails before any of the new page-table verification can be used. The change also removes boot, CPU-local, trap, task, serial, PCI, and initialization behavior from the executable architecture merely by commenting it out.
- **Suggestion:** Restore the original module declarations and architecture entry-point implementations unchanged. If individual modules cannot yet pass the verification frontend, exclude or annotate only the minimum verification boundary needed, while preserving the original executable Rust and recording any required rewrite with the mandated `Origin Rust:` form.

## Medium

No evidence-backed medium-severity findings.

## Low

No useful low-severity findings.

## Evidence check record

- Read `diff.patch` in full scope and compared the affected LoongArch module against both `before/` and `after/` context.
- Refutation check: searched the after tree for consumers of the removed modules and entry points. The cited shared call sites remain active and are not guarded away from `target_arch = "loongarch64"`.
- Contract/proof review included the changed `PageTableEntryTrait::set_prop` contract, architecture-specific `set_prop_ensures` predicates, LoongArch page-table preconditions and postconditions, the added trusted hardware-reader boundary, and the changed kernel-range facts. No additional high/medium finding was retained without stronger caller-impact evidence.
- No `#[verifier::rlimit(...)]` change appears in the patch, so the `rlimit > 200` workflow check was not triggered.
- No newly added or materially changed external specification for a `std`, `core`, or `alloc` API appears in the patch, so the upstream-spec workflow check was not triggered.
- **No-verification disclosure:** Per the requested fast-review override, I did not run Verus, compile the LoongArch target, execute caller experiments, inspect repository history, delegate persona passes, or perform the exhaustive guideline checklist. The blocking result above is based on direct before/after source and unresolved-call-site evidence.

# Review: PR 868 snapshot

> Scope: `diff.patch` is the authoritative change set; `before/` and `after/` were used only for immediate source context. Fast isolated review of maintainability, proof/trust boundaries, assumptions, API contracts, invariants, rlimit values above 200, and specification reuse.

**Bottom line:** No strong, evidence-backed review finding was identified. The patch adds a focused bridge from `relate_region` to `LinkedListOwner::inv`, exposes the resulting invariant and region well-formedness in the `push_front`/`push_back` contracts, and records mutable-reference alias preservation needed by the back-insertion call chain. The sole visible rlimit is an unchanged value of 200, not a newly introduced or over-cap value.

## High

No findings.

## Medium

No findings.

## Low

| Finding | Guideline | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| None | — | No useful low-severity issue was supported by the reviewed evidence. |

## Evidence check record

- **Invariant bridge:** `ostd/specs/mm/frame/linked_list/linked_list_owners.rs:245-253` defines `LinkedListOwner::inv` as the list-id condition, permission-vector lengths, and per-index `inv_at`. `relate_region` supplies the same shape conditions and a per-index `relate_region_at` (`:319-335`), while `relate_region_at` includes both clauses of `inv_at` (`:315-316`). The added lemma at `:350-362` therefore matches the existing predicate definitions and centralizes a reusable implication rather than duplicating caller proofs.
- **Push contracts:** `ostd/src/mm/frame/linked_list.rs:257-280` and `:352-379` add `wf_region` and owner-invariant postconditions to `push_front` and `push_back`. Their bodies recover the post-insertion owner, invoke the new bridge lemma, and retain the established region relation; the `push_back` path also explicitly establishes `self.wf_region`.
- **Alias-preservation contracts:** `ostd/src/mm/frame/linked_list.rs:642-650` states that the returned ghost cursor's list is the same mutable list at return and final states. `insert_before` propagates that relationship at `:1197-1200`, supporting the `push_back` receiver after mutation without adding a trust annotation or assumption.
- **`pop_front` rewrite:** `ostd/src/mm/frame/linked_list.rs:303-308` merely groups the two existing `Some`-case guarantees under one implication; no precondition or promised result is removed.
- **Trust and assumptions:** The patch adds no `external_body`, `assume`, `admit`, or other trust-boundary escape. The nearby pre-existing `lazy_get_id` assumption is outside the changed hunks.
- **Rlimit:** The authoritative patch contains no added, removed, or changed `#[verifier::rlimit(...)]`. The surrounding `insert_before` remains at exactly 200 (`ostd/src/mm/frame/linked_list.rs:1186-1188`), so there is no value above the requested cap.
- **Specification reuse:** The new `lemma_relate_region_implies_inv` is a local, reusable proof lemma over project-specific linked-list ownership predicates. No new external specification for `std`, `core`, or `alloc` is introduced.
- **Verification disclosure:** Per the fast-review instruction, no Verus run, build, tests, history inspection, exhaustive guideline pass, or isolated caller experiment was performed. Conclusions are static and limited to `diff.patch` plus the supplied before/after context.

issues.description: The LinkedList pop_front and pop_back contracts consume the tracked list owner by value but return only the removed frame owner, leaving callers without the permissions needed to keep using the remaining list.
issues.rationale: LinkedListOwner is a tracked struct carrying exclusive representation and metadata permissions. Both pop methods accept it by value, move it into a local CursorOwner, then return only take_current's Option<(UniqueFrame, Tracked<UniqueFrameOwner>)>. take_current updates its borrowed CursorOwner in place, but the enclosing pop method neither returns that owner nor borrows the caller's owner slot. Thus even a successful pop on a multi-element list loses the caller's ownership handle to the remaining elements, preventing a subsequent verified pop/push using the same list resource. The direct child repair changes the argument to &mut LinkedListOwner, explicitly restores cursor.list_own through tracked_restore_list_owner, and exposes the resulting list/region relationship. This is a verification API resource-flow defect, not a claim of runtime corruption. It already exists in the comparison base and is captured here as the PR-internal pre-repair snapshot, not claimed to be introduced by the initial push_front changes.

Read both complete pop wrappers, take_current signature/postconditions/body, tracked owner declaration and constructors, direct repair diff and prior archive audit. > Fast, non-exhaustive review against the VOSTD maintainability, proof-engineering, API-contract, and narrowly scoped workflow criteria.
> Scope: the immutable 153-line `diff.patch`, covering `ostd/src/arch/x86/mod.rs` and `ostd/src/arch/x86/task/mod.rs`, with the supplied `before/` and `after/` trees used only for surrounding context.

**Bottom line:** The added contracts are direct models of the affected field updates, and the diff introduces no assumptions, admits, external specifications, or `#[verifier::rlimit]` changes. One maintainability issue should be fixed before merge: the verification patch unnecessarily rewrites the executable bodies of both constructors instead of preserving the original Rust.

## High

None.

## Medium

### Preserve the executable constructor bodies

- **Guideline:** `preserve-exec-code`
- **Location:** `ostd/src/arch/x86/task/mod.rs:44` and `ostd/src/arch/x86/task/mod.rs:90`
- **Quoted evidence:** Before, `TaskContext::new` used `Self {` followed by separate `regs:`, `rip:`, and `fsbase:` lines; after, line 45 is `Self { regs: CalleeRegs::new(), rip: 0, fsbase: 0 }`. Before, `CalleeRegs::new` likewise placed `rsp` through `r15` on separate lines; after, line 91 is `CalleeRegs { rsp: 0, rbx: 0, rbp: 0, r12: 0, r13: 0, r14: 0, r15: 0 }`. The diff gives no Verus-required reason and retains no adjacent `Origin Rust:` record.
- **Problem:** VOSTD's `preserve-exec-code` rule requires verification changes to leave executable Rust intact unless Verus forces a minimal rewrite. These formatting rewrites add review noise and make it harder to distinguish proof-only changes from runtime changes.
- **Suggestion:** Restore both constructor bodies byte-for-byte to their original multiline forms and leave only the surrounding verification attributes and contracts as additions.

## Low

None.

## Evidence check record

- Read all 153 lines of `diff.patch` and compared each changed file with its supplied `before/` and `after/` versions.
- Checked the new `TaskContextView` and every added contract against the executable field assignments. The setters preserve all fields not named in their struct update, the getters return the represented fields, and on the x86-64 target the `usize`/`u64` stack-pointer conversions do not introduce a contract mismatch.
- Inspected the surrounding `TaskContextApi` declaration and representative callers. No strong evidence showed that the added implementation contracts overstate accepted inputs or returned state.
- Searched the scoped diff for `assume`, `admit`, trusted/external bodies, external `std`/`core`/`alloc` specifications, and `#[verifier::rlimit]`; none were introduced. Consequently, there is no rlimit-over-200 or upstream-spec-reuse finding.
- Searched the supplied tree for uses of the new model. `TaskContextView` is used by the constructor and accessor contracts, so it is not an unused speculative helper.
- Per the requested fast-review scope, I did not inspect Git history, run Verus or CI, execute isolated caller experiments, or perform the exhaustive persona/checklist workflow. Findings are therefore based on static source evidence only.

# Review: PR #871 (`diff.patch`, head snapshot `61c301b7f35d`)

> Fast isolated review of the authoritative patch plus the supplied `before/` and `after/` context. The patch contains CI, Python, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS changes only; it changes no Verus proof/API contract, trusted external specification, or `#[verifier::rlimit]` setting.

**Bottom line:** The new dashboard can publish materially false verification-coverage data because per-file `line_count` failures are converted into zero-valued reports while the snapshot command still succeeds. The workflow is also not idempotent for an unchanged rerun, and its advertised parallelism is never used, making the new 30-minute job unnecessarily vulnerable to timeout. The first issue should block publication until failures abort snapshot generation.

## High

### Failed `line_count` runs are published as valid zero coverage

- **Category:** Assumption / publication invariant
- **Location:** `tools/verus_stats.py:247-269`, `tools/verus_stats.py:285-307`, `tools/verus_stats.py:437-461`
- **Evidence:** `run_line_count_file` returns `(None, error)` on a nonzero exit or invalid JSON. `collect_coverage` nevertheless stores that `None` in `vostd_reports` or `mainline_reports`, and `classify_lines(None)` returns all-zero buckets. The error is only appended to `warnings`; `cmd_snapshot` writes the snapshot and returns `0` after `print_report(modules, warnings)`.
- **Problem:** A failed VOSTD count is presented as unverified whenever its mainline twin succeeds; a failed mainline count can clamp a successfully counted VOSTD file to a zero budget and remove it from the emitted module list. A partial tool failure therefore produces a green CI job and a misleading verification dashboard instead of withholding invalid data.
- **Suggestion:** Treat every per-file `line_count` error as fatal before `write_snapshot`, reporting all affected paths and exiting nonzero. If partial results are intentionally supported, represent failed files explicitly and prevent totals/snapshots from being published as coverage until the dataset is complete.

## Medium

### An unchanged workflow rerun fails at `git commit`

- **Category:** Maintainability / idempotent publication contract
- **Location:** `.github/workflows/ci.yml:391-414`, `tools/verus_stats.py:480-488`
- **Evidence:** `cmd_record` explicitly updates an existing point for the same SHA (`existing.update(point)  # reruns refresh the same commit`), after which the workflow copies the snapshot and unconditionally runs `git ... commit`. With the same snapshot and history bytes, Git exits nonzero with nothing to commit, and `set -e` terminates the job before the push/deployment path.
- **Problem:** Re-running a successful workflow for the same commit is a normal supported operation, but an unchanged rerun makes `perf-history` fail and consequently prevents `doc-deploy` from satisfying its success dependency.
- **Suggestion:** Test whether `git diff --cached --quiet` after `git add stats`; commit and push only when data changed, otherwise report that the SHA is already recorded and continue successfully.

### `--jobs` does not parallelize any counting work

- **Category:** Maintainability / resource-bound assumption
- **Location:** `tools/verus_stats.py:251-269`
- **Evidence:** A `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=jobs)` is created as `pool`, but `pool.submit`, `pool.map`, and the `pool` variable are never used. Both list comprehensions invoke `run_line_count_file(...)` directly and sequentially before their result loops begin.
- **Problem:** The CLI and implementation imply bounded parallel counting, but every VOSTD and mainline Rust file starts a separate `line_count` process serially. This can needlessly exhaust the new job's 30-minute timeout as the source tree grows.
- **Suggestion:** Submit each keyed file to the executor (or use `pool.map`) and collect futures deterministically; alternatively remove `--jobs` and size the CI timeout for an explicitly sequential implementation.

## Low

No evidence-backed low-severity findings.

## Evidence check record

- Read all 1,518 lines of `diff.patch` and inspected the cited files in the supplied `after/` tree with line-numbered context; consulted the corresponding `before/` tree for scope (all three cited implementations are newly introduced).
- Searched the authoritative patch for Verus proof/API changes, trusted/external specifications, and `#[verifier::rlimit]` changes. None are present, so proof reuse, trusted-model soundness, API pre/postcondition, upstream-spec, and rlimit-cap checks are not applicable.
- Refutation check for the High finding: confirmed `classify_lines(None)` produces zeros, failed reports remain present in the report dictionaries, warnings do not alter the exit status, and snapshot emission precedes the successful return.
- Refutation check for rerun idempotence: confirmed same-SHA history entries are updated in place, while the workflow has no staged-diff guard around the unconditional commit.
- Refutation check for parallelism: confirmed the executor object has no consumer and both subprocess calls occur inside ordinary eager list comprehensions.
- Per the requested fast-review override, no history inspection, Verus invocation, tests, browser checks, or isolated experiments were performed. Conclusions are static-review findings only; CI/verification was not rerun.

# Review: `diff.patch` (`before` → `after` snapshots)

> Produced from the supplied VOSTD review skill, `diff.patch`, and the matching before/after source snapshots.
> Scope: authoritative patch SHA-256 `d6129143d3f8201bfea95035780acdd9f1b32edc639de19a5935be01ddd03d5d`; changed files `ostd/src/arch/x86/ex_table.rs` and `ostd/src/arch/x86/mod.rs`.

**Bottom line:** The lookup contract is caller-usable and describes the first matching exception-table entry without an apparent precondition or postcondition gap. The main issue is architectural: the patch introduces an uninterpreted model and an `external_body` axiom in the executable module next to the verified caller, expanding a locally owned trust boundary instead of centralizing it. No high-severity issue was found in the supplied patch.

## High

None.

## Medium

### Centralize the exception-table trust boundary

- **Guideline:** `centralize-trusted-boundaries`
- **Location:** `ostd/src/arch/x86/ex_table.rs:23`, `ostd/src/arch/x86/ex_table.rs:125`

# Review: PR 887 snapshot `431e3c7c0000`

> Produced from `diff.patch`, the captured `before/` and `after/` trees, and the VOSTD review skill's maintainability, proof-engineering, and API-contract criteria.
> Scope: fast, non-exhaustive static review of the changes represented by `diff.patch`; no history inspection, caller experiment, Verus run, or CI verification was performed.

**Bottom line:** The patch cannot merge in its current form because it makes verification progress by removing core x86 execution paths from the compiled crate: CPU-local storage, exception construction, context execution, FPU handling, trap initialization/dispatch, and the public `UserMode` implementation are all wrapped in comments. This is a direct violation of `preserve-exec-code` and materially changes the runtime/API surface. Separately, the new trusted `wrfsbase` boundary is left inside the verified implementation instead of being isolated as an external specification.

## High

### H1 — Verification comments out production x86 functionality

- **Guideline:** `preserve-exec-code`
- **Locations:** `ostd/src/arch/x86/cpu/mod.rs:4`, `ostd/src/arch/x86/cpu/context/mod.rs:170`, `ostd/src/arch/x86/cpu/context/mod.rs:361`, `ostd/src/arch/x86/cpu/context/mod.rs:669`, `ostd/src/arch/x86/trap/mod.rs:26`, `ostd/src/arch/x86/trap/mod.rs:117`, `ostd/src/arch/x86/trap/mod.rs:156`, `ostd/src/user.rs:5`, `ostd/src/user.rs:96`
- **Evidence:** The after-tree contains `/* GS storage awaits ... Origin Rust: pub mod local; */`; wraps `CpuException::new` in a block comment; wraps `impl UserContextApiInternal for UserContext` (including execution and trap-frame construction) in a block comment; wraps the FPU implementation in a block comment; wraps the trap submodules, `init`, and all trap dispatch in block comments; and wraps `UserContextApiInternal`, `UserMode`, and `ReturnReason` in block comments. In the before-tree these are live compiled items, for example `pub mod local;` at `ostd/src/arch/x86/cpu/mod.rs:4`, `pub(crate) fn new(...)` at `ostd/src/arch/x86/cpu/context/mod.rs:148`, trap modules at `ostd/src/arch/x86/trap/mod.rs:17-19`, and `pub struct UserMode` at `ostd/src/user.rs:61`.
- **Problem:** This is not a proof-only change. It deletes the kernel's CPU-local, exception, user-mode execution, FPU, trap initialization, and trap-handling paths from compilation and removes public user-mode APIs. The module comments acknowledge the missing contracts, but missing verification support does not justify changing executable behavior or the exported API.
- **Suggestion:** Restore the executable code and module declarations exactly in place. Restrict `#[verus_verify]` to the subset that can currently be verified, and isolate unsupported dependencies with the narrowest permitted external specifications or verification boundaries without commenting out their callers or runtime implementations. If some code truly must be changed for Verus, keep the change minimal and demonstrate runtime equivalence to the original.

## Medium

### M1 — `activate_tls_pointer` introduces a local trusted body instead of an external model

- **Guideline:** `centralize-trusted-boundaries`
- **Location:** `ostd/src/arch/x86/cpu/context/mod.rs:354`
- **Evidence:** The new method annotation is `#[verus_verify(external_body)]` followed by an empty `#[verus_spec]`, while its body directly executes `unsafe { wrfsbase(self.fsbase() as u64) }`.
- **Problem:** The verified implementation now carries an opaque trusted body locally. Although the rustdoc admits that no hardware-state postcondition is modeled, leaving the trust marker on the caller-facing wrapper obscures the exact external operation being trusted and makes future callers depend on a boundary that cannot be reused or audited independently.
- **Suggestion:** Put the `wrfsbase` trust boundary in the repository's external-specification layer with the original signature and the narrowest truthful contract, then keep `activate_tls_pointer` as ordinary executable code verified against that specification. If no meaningful hardware-state model exists yet, explicitly model only the absence of a usable postcondition rather than marking the whole wrapper external.

## Low

No low-severity findings.

## Evidence check record

- Read all 736 lines of `diff.patch` and inspected the cited `before/` and `after/` source around each changed region.
- Confirmed that the removed functionality is live executable code in `before/` and block-commented in `after/`; H1 does not rely on a build failure inference.
- Searched the changed after-tree for `external_body`, `uninterp`, `axiom`, `assume`, `admit`, and `#[verifier::rlimit]`. The CPU-count uninterpreted function and bounds axiom are moved from `ostd/src/cpu/mod.rs` to `ostd/specs/cpu.rs` without a material semantic change. No changed `rlimit` above 200 was found.
- Reviewed the new `UserContextApi` trait contracts and concrete implementation statically; no strong precondition or postcondition defect was established in this fast pass.
- No claim was made that the patch fails Verus or CI. Per the requested fast-review constraints, no Verus verification, compilation, history analysis, exhaustive guideline checklist, caller experiment, or external source lookup was performed; conclusions are limited to the quoted static evidence.

# Review: PR 890 snapshot `5b1e96c2ec18`

> Produced from the supplied `diff.patch`, with `before/` and `after/` used only for line-numbered context.
> Scope: two changed files: `ostd/src/task/scheduler/info.rs` and `ostd/src/util/ops.rs`. This fast review covers maintainability, proof/trust assumptions, API contracts and invariants, `rlimit > 200`, and spec reuse.

**Bottom line:** The new `lemma_filter_laws` does not have a parameter named `iter`, but its contract and body reference `iter`, while its only call supplies `iter` as a third argument. This is a direct compile/verification blocker in the changed code. The other contract change usefully makes the iterator-law guarantee unconditional, and the new `set_if_is_none` equivalence closes the success/failure result contract without exposing an evident invariant gap.

## High

### `lemma_filter_laws` has an inconsistent signature and call

- **Guideline:** `preserve-exec-code` / proof-engineering correctness
- **Location:** `ostd/src/util/ops.rs:141` and `ostd/src/util/ops.rs:148`
- **Evidence:** The call is `lemma_filter_laws(iter, pred, ret);`, but the added signature declares only `pred: P` and `ret: core::iter::Filter<I, P>`. Its `requires` and body nevertheless use the undeclared name `iter`:

  ```rust
  proof fn lemma_filter_laws<I: Iterator, P: FnMut(&I::Item) -> bool>(
      pred: P,
      ret: core::iter::Filter<I, P>,
  )
      requires
          iter.obeys_prophetic_iter_laws(),
          filter_post(iter, pred, ret),
  {
      filter_postcondition(iter, pred, ret);
  }
  ```

  Thus the helper both references an unbound value and is called with the wrong arity.

# Review: PR 897 isolated patch

> Produced from the supplied `diff.patch`, its `before/` and `after/` snapshots, and the VOSTD review skill's proof-engineering and API-contract criteria.
> Scope: fast, non-exhaustive review of `diff.patch` in `vostd-pr-test/pr-897-657bce05372e`; no repository history, sub-reviewers, Verus runs, exhaustive checklist, or caller experiments were used.

**Bottom line:** The GAT consolidation itself is coherent, but it also removes the generic validity guarantees that made a `NonNullPtr` permission and borrowed reference usable through the trait. The concrete `Box` and `Arc` implementations partially recover those facts inside their predicates, while the `Frame` implementation makes validity conditional; generic RCU clients therefore no longer receive a contract establishing that the returned reference is valid. This should be repaired before merge at the trait boundary, rather than relying on implementation-specific predicates.

## High

None.

## Medium

### The consolidated trait no longer guarantees valid permissions or references

- **Guidelines:** `complete-external-contracts`, `api-postconditions`
- **Location:** `ostd/src/sync/rcu/non_null/mod.rs:43`
- **Quoted evidence:** The new trait declares `type Ref<'a>: 'a;`, `type Permission;`, and `type RefPermission<'a>;` (lines 43, 47, and 53), where the old declarations required `Permission: Inv`, `RefPermission: Inv`, and supplied validity obligations. The new `raw_as_ref` contract at lines 135-143 requires only `ptr_perm_match(...)` and ensures only `ref_rel_perm(ret, perm@)`; it no longer requires `perm@.inv()` or guarantees a valid returned reference. Likewise, `into_raw`, `from_raw`, `borrow_ref_perm`, `borrow_perm_as_ref_perm`, and `ref_as_raw` all lose their former `inv()` clauses.
- **Problem:** This is not merely moving validity into a common predicate. `Box` and `Arc` explicitly add `perm.inv()` to `ptr_perm_match`/`ref_rel_perm`, but `Frame::ptr_perm_match` at `ostd/src/mm/frame/frame_ref.rs:205-209` checks only the slot pointer, slot address, and initialization. `Frame::ref_rel_perm` at lines 222-227 is the implication `r.inv() ==> { perm.inv() && ... }`, so when `r.inv()` is unavailable it provides no validity fact. Consequently, generic RCU paths such as `RcuInner::read_with` (`ostd/src/sync/rcu/mod.rs:430-466`) can return `P::Ref<'a>` after proving `ptr_perm_match`, but their callable contracts no longer establish that the permission or returned reference satisfies its invariant. This weakens the abstraction precisely at the unsafe conversion boundary and prevents natural generic callers from recovering the reference's modeled contents and safety invariant.
- **Suggestion:** Restore a trait-level validity obligation. The direct repair is to retain `Permission: Inv`, `RefPermission<'a>: Inv`, and `Ref<'a>: Inv`, restore the removed `inv()` pre/postconditions (including the ref-permission-to-owned-permission lemma), and make `raw_as_ref` guarantee `ret.inv()`. If the GAT implementation cannot express those bounds, introduce one explicit trait predicate for owned-permission validity and one for reference validity, require/preserve them in every conversion and borrow method, and make `Frame::ptr_perm_match` or the conversion contracts include the full `FrameRawPerms::inv()` facts rather than a conditional implication.

## Low

None.

## Evidence check record

- Read all 913 lines of `diff.patch` and checked the affected trait and `Frame`/`Either` implementations against their `before/` and `after/` context.
- Refutation check: `Box<T>` and `Arc<T>` do place `perm.inv()` in their new `ptr_perm_match` and `ref_rel_perm` predicates, but that does not repair the generic contract, and the changed `Frame` predicates do not unconditionally imply either permission or reference validity.
- Invariant check: `FrameRawPerms::inv()` additionally requires a full fractional permission and `MetaSlot::perms_related`; those facts are absent from `Frame::ptr_perm_match`, which only carries address/initialization facts.
- Reuse/spec check: the patch introduces no competing standard-library external specification. The new `FrameRawPermsRef` reuses `FrameRawPerms` as its view and implements `Inv`; no separate evidence-backed specification-reuse finding was found.
- Workflow check: the patch contains no added or changed `#[verifier::rlimit(...)]`, so there is no `rlimit > 200` finding. It also contains no newly added or materially changed external specification for a `std`, `core`, or `alloc` API.
- Assumption/trust check: no newly added `assume`, `admit`, `external_body`, or axiom was found in the patch. The change does remove invariant obligations from a trusted unsafe trait boundary, as reported above.
- **No-verification disclosure:** This fast isolated pass did not run Verus, Rust tests, CI, or any synthetic client experiment. Conclusions are based only on static contract and source comparison; the supplied task treats verification as out of scope.

# Review: PR #900 snapshot `d5d5a579f00c`

> Produced from the VOSTD coding-guideline review criteria and the skill's API-contract criteria.
> Scope: the authoritative `diff.patch`, with `before/` and `after/` used only for surrounding context and source line numbers.

**Bottom line:** The new `Drop` implementation makes local-IRQ restoration operational, but its correctness depends on guards being destroyed in LIFO order even though the safe API does not enforce that order. A safe caller can therefore leave one `DisabledLocalIrqGuard` alive while an earlier guard re-enables interrupts, invalidating the guard and lock atomicity invariants. This should be fixed before merge with restoration state that is robust to safe out-of-order destruction, or with an API that structurally enforces nesting.

## High

### A live IRQ guard does not guarantee that IRQs remain disabled

- **Guideline:** `api-preconditions`
- **Location:** `ostd/src/trap/irq.rs:277`
- **Evidence:** The changed documentation says, “`Nested guards must be dropped in reverse order`” (`ostd/src/trap/irq.rs:202-203`), while the newly enabled destructor executes `if self.was_enabled { irq::enable_local(); }` (`ostd/src/trap/irq.rs:277-281`). Construction records the current flag independently for each guard (`let was_enabled = irq::is_local_enabled(); ... Self { was_enabled }`, lines 251-257). Thus safe code can create `outer` while IRQs are enabled, create `inner` while they are disabled, and then call `drop(outer)` before `drop(inner)`; dropping `outer` enables IRQs while `inner` remains live. `DisabledPreemptGuard` now embeds this same guard (`ostd/src/task/preempt/guard.rs:108-110`), and `PreemptDisabled` lock guardians obtain it through `disable_preempt()` (`ostd/src/task/preempt/guard.rs:136-141`).
- **Problem:** LIFO destruction is a correctness precondition for the new runtime behavior, but it is neither expressed nor enforced by the safe API. This can break the advertised disabled-IRQ/preemption state while protected code or a spin-lock guard is still active, allowing interrupt re-entry into a region whose atomicity depends on that state.
- **Suggestion:** Make restoration robust to arbitrary safe drop order, for example by maintaining per-CPU IRQ-guard depth plus the state to restore when the depth reaches zero. Alternatively, redesign acquisition so the type/lifetime structure enforces properly nested destruction; documentation alone is insufficient for a safety-critical invariant exposed through safe `drop`.

## Medium

No medium-severity findings.

## Low

No low-severity findings.

## Evidence check record

- Read all 470 lines of `diff.patch`; inspected the corresponding before/after context for `cpu_core.rs`, `arch/x86/irq.rs`, `task/preempt/guard.rs`, `trap/irq.rs`, and the affected `SpinGuardian` definitions and call sites.
- Confirmed statically that the LIFO condition is documented but not encoded in ownership or lifetimes, and that `Drop` can re-enable IRQs solely from an individual guard's captured `was_enabled` bit.
- No `#[verifier::rlimit(...)]` change is present, and no new or materially changed external specification for a `std`, `core`, or `alloc` API is present.
- Per the requested fast review override, no history inspection, Verus run, build, test, exhaustive-rule enumeration, or isolated caller experiment was performed. The finding is based on direct control-flow and safe-Rust destruction semantics; verification status was not independently checked.

# Review: PR 909 snapshot `diff.patch`

> Produced from the supplied patch and its `before/` and `after/` source snapshots, using the VOSTD maintainability, proof-engineering, API-contract, and narrowly applicable workflow criteria.
> Scope: fast non-exhaustive review of `pr-909-a2d5bf577533/diff.patch`; no repository history, sub-reviewers, Verus runs, caller experiments, or exhaustive checklist pass.

**Bottom line:** The revised `Arc<T>` implementation does not preserve the permission that justifies its borrowed raw-pointer view. It reconstructs an `Arc` without passing the owning permission required by the trusted `arc_from_raw` contract, and later obtains a new owning permission for the same runtime strong reference before converting that permission into a static borrow. This breaks the proof-level ownership story at a trusted boundary and should block merging until the round trip carries the original borrowed permission end to end.

## High

### The `Arc` borrowed round trip discards the input permission and manufactures a replacement

- **Guidelines:** `complete-external-contracts`, `centralize-trusted-boundaries`
- **Location:** `ostd/src/sync/rcu/non_null/mod.rs:454`
- **Evidence:** The trait requires `raw_as_ref` to receive a borrowed reading permission (`Tracked<Self::RefPermission<'a>>`), and the `Arc` implementation defines that permission as `&'a ArcPointsTo<T>` (`mod.rs:393`). The changed implementation destructures it as `Tracked(perm)` but never uses it:

  ```rust
  unsafe fn raw_as_ref<'a>(
      raw: NonNull<Self::Target>,
      Tracked(perm): Tracked<Self::RefPermission<'a>>,
  ) -> Self::Ref<'a> {
      unsafe {
          // TODO: Model borrowed construction; arc_from_raw requires an owning token.
          ArcRef { inner: ManuallyDrop::new(arc_from_raw(raw.as_ptr())), _marker: PhantomData }
      }
  }
  ```

  The called trusted wrapper explicitly requires an owning ghost input (`verified_libs/vstd_extra/src/external/smart_ptr.rs:291-301`):

  ```rust
  with Tracked(points_to): Tracked<ArcPointsTo<T>>,
  requires
      points_to.ptr() == ptr,
      points_to.is_init(),
  ```

  The reverse conversion then calls `arc_into_raw` to obtain a fresh `owned_perm` and immortalizes it as a shared permission (`mod.rs:471-476`):

  ```rust
  proof_decl! { let tracked owned_perm: ArcPointsTo<T>; }
  let ptr = (#[verus_spec(with => Tracked(owned_perm))]
  arc_into_raw(ManuallyDrop::into_inner(ptr_ref.inner))).cast_mut();
  proof_decl! { let tracked perm = tracked_static_ref(owned_perm); }
  ```

- **Problem:** At runtime, `raw_as_ref`/`ref_as_raw` merely borrow and round-trip the single strong reference represented by the original raw pointer. At proof level, however, the changed code stops connecting reconstruction to the original permission and asks the external `arc_into_raw` model for another owning `ArcPointsTo` token for that same runtime reference. Turning the replacement into a static tracked reference does not restore the missing relationship to the caller's original borrow; it leaves two proof resources describing one strong reference and can outlive consumption of the original owner.
- **Suggestion:** Carry the original `&'a ArcPointsTo<T>` inside `ArcRef` as a tracked field and return that exact borrow from `ref_as_raw`, as the `BoxRef` design does. If Verus cannot specify the runtime `Arc::from_raw`/`Arc::into_raw` borrowed round trip directly, add one narrowly scoped trusted wrapper in `vstd_extra::external` whose contract takes and returns the same borrowed permission and exposes pointer identity; do not obtain a second owning `ArcPointsTo` token.

## Medium

### A generic alignment fact is strengthened through local axioms instead of the external-model boundary

- **Guideline:** `centralize-trusted-boundaries`
- **Location:** `ostd/src/sync/rcu/non_null/mod.rs:114`
- **Evidence:** The patch strengthens `lemma_align_bits_range` so every implementation must establish `Self::align_bits_inv()` (`mod.rs:114-119`). For `Box<T>` and `Arc<T>`, the new invariant equates an externally defined constant to Verus layout (`mod.rs:229-234`, `395-400`), while the implementations discharge the stronger contract with local axioms (`mod.rs:284-285`, `436-437`):

  ```rust
  #[verifier::external_body]
  const ALIGN_BITS: u32 = core::mem::align_of::<T>().trailing_zeros();

  open spec fn align_bits_inv() -> bool {
      1usize << Self::ALIGN_BITS == vstd::layout::align_of::<T>()
  }

  axiom fn lemma_align_bits_range();
  ```

- **Problem:** The patch replaces caller-local `assume` statements with a reusable fact, but the fact remains trusted twice in an ordinary OSTD implementation. Its truth depends on the external Rust constant and layout model, so keeping duplicate generic axioms here obscures the actual trust boundary and permits the two implementations to drift.
- **Suggestion:** Specify the `align_of::<T>().trailing_zeros()` relationship once in the external specification layer (or reuse an existing vstd layout theorem if available), then prove both trait implementations from that single boundary fact.

## Low

| Finding | Guideline | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| Propose the new `NonNull::eq` model upstream | `upstream-reusable-specs` | `verified_libs/vstd_extra/src/external/nonnull.rs:10-18` adds a generic external specification for a `core` API. Because this model is broadly reusable and otherwise becomes a second long-lived trust source, submit it to Verus/vstd (or document the upstream tracking issue) rather than leaving it only in OSTD's external-spec layer. |

## Evidence check record

- Read the complete supplied `diff.patch`, then checked the relevant `before/` and `after/` definitions of `NonNullPtr`, `ArcRef`, `ArcPointsTo`, `arc_into_raw`, and `arc_from_raw`.
- Confirmed that the old `raw_as_ref` explicitly supplied its `ArcPointsTo` token to `arc_from_raw`, while the new version removes that `#[verus_spec(with perm)]` connection.
- Confirmed that `arc_into_raw`'s external contract returns an owning `ArcPointsTo<T>` and `arc_from_raw`'s external contract consumes one; the changed round trip instead converts the newly returned owner into a static tracked reference.
- Confirmed that no `#[verifier::rlimit(...)]` change appears in the patch, so there is no `rlimit > 200` finding.
- No claim was based on verification output. # Review: PR #915 snapshot (`diff.patch`)

> Produced from the VOSTD maintainability, proof-engineering, workflow, and API-contract criteria.
> Scope: `pr-915-7a42b67bb385/diff.patch` is the authoritative change set; files under `before/` and `after/` were used only for surrounding context. Per the fast-review request, history, exhaustive rule enumeration, Verus/CI runs, caller experiments, and subagent passes were not performed.

**Bottom line:** The newly verified address conversions prove their bodies by assuming range predicates that are false for values admitted by their own public `From<usize>` implementations. Because these assumptions occur inside ordinary safe, generic `From` conversions, any verified caller can reach them with an unrestricted value and make the proof context inconsistent. This is a trust-boundary and API-contract blocker; the range must be established structurally or checked at the input boundary rather than assumed locally.

## High

### Unrestricted values reach unconditional trusted range assumptions

- **Guidelines:** `centralize-trusted-boundaries`, `api-preconditions`, `api-postconditions`
- **Location:** `ostd/libs/linux-bzimage/builder/src/mapping.rs:124` (especially lines 125–138), and `ostd/libs/linux-bzimage/builder/src/mapping.rs:143` (especially lines 144–155)
- **Evidence:** The module exposes unrestricted construction with `impl From<usize> for SetupVA` and `impl From<usize> for SetupFileOffset` (lines 48–53 and 86–91). Nevertheless, the first cross-type conversion executes `assume(SETUP32_LMA - LEGACY_SETUP_SEC_SIZE <= va.addr <= usize::MAX - LEGACY_SETUP_SEC_SIZE);` (line 134), and the reverse conversion executes `assume(offset.offset <= usize::MAX - SETUP32_LMA);` (line 152). The module documentation itself confirms that “unrestricted integer construction does not enforce” these ranges (lines 9–10). The formal postconditions are only implications (lines 125–129 and 144–148), while both `FromSpecImpl` instances declare `obeys_from_spec() -> bool { true }` (lines 162–179).
- **Problem:** These are not facts about every `SetupVA` or `SetupFileOffset`; for example, `SetupVA::from(0)` violates the first assumed lower bound, and `SetupFileOffset::from(usize::MAX)` violates the second assumed upper bound. Putting the assumptions inside safe `From` implementations allows an arbitrary verified caller to introduce a false proposition, after which unrelated obligations can be proved. The conditional result clauses do not contain the damage because the unconditional `assume` is available while verifying the function body, and the total-looking `From` API does not require callers to establish the antecedent.
- **Suggestion:** Remove both local assumptions. Encode valid mapped addresses/offsets in construction—e.g. checked `TryFrom<usize>`/validated constructors plus a representation invariant—and make the cross-type conversion available only for validated values; alternatively make the conversion itself checked and return `Option`/`Result`. If ELF provenance truly must remain trusted, centralize that fact at the ELF-validation boundary (or in the designated external-spec boundary) and return a validated mapping type from that boundary. Give the resulting API an unconditional exact postcondition for successful conversion; do not advertise an unrestricted, always-obeying `FromSpecImpl` unless the operation is total for every constructible source value.

## Medium

No medium-severity findings.

## Low

No low-severity findings.

## Evidence check record

- Read all 575 lines of the authoritative `diff.patch` and the complete before/after `mapping.rs` files.
- Checked direct callers in `builder/src/lib.rs:91–93` and `builder/src/pe_header.rs:368–375`; both obtain values from ELF data, but neither changes the fact that the public constructors admit arbitrary `usize` values and the conversion implementations assume the ranges unconditionally.
- Searched the scoped patch and after-tree for `assume`, `admit`, `external_body`, and `rlimit`. The only scoped trust operations are the two assumptions reported above; no changed `#[verifier::rlimit(...)]` exists, so the `rlimit > 200` workflow check did not trigger.
- The patch adds no external specification for a `std`, `core`, or `alloc` API, so the upstreamable-spec workflow check did not trigger. The added `FromSpecImpl`, `AddSpecImpl`, and `SubSpecImpl` implementations reuse vstd interfaces rather than introducing a parallel interface.
- No Verus verification, compilation, CI run, runtime test, or isolated caller experiment was performed, as required by the fast-review override. Findings are based solely on static source and contract evidence.

issues.rationale: Each implementation unconditionally assumes the exact bound used as the antecedent, so the function can and should expose the exact conversion relation unconditionally to callers. The reviewer flags both directions, and the final approved head replaces both implications with unconditional equality postconditions. This is a contract-strength/clarity issue rather than a claim that the accepted normal-build trust assumptions are invalid.

# Review: PR 92 captured patch

> Produced from the authoritative `diff.patch` and the captured before/after source context. Scope: the three changed files under `lock-protocol/src/mm/page_table/` in `pr-92-8fe6908fea09`.

**Bottom line:** The new `from_raw_paddr` postcondition claims a bounded physical address for every possible input, although the API has no corresponding precondition. This either makes a conforming implementation impossible to verify for out-of-range inputs or, if an implementation is trusted, exposes an unjustified fact to every caller. No other strong, evidence-backed issue was found in the captured patch.

## High

None.

## Medium

### `from_raw_paddr` promises well-formedness for arbitrary addresses

- **Guideline:** `api-preconditions`
- **Location:** `lock-protocol/src/mm/page_table/node/mod.rs:134`
- **Evidence:** The newly added predicate is `self.paddr() < exec::PHYSICAL_BASE_ADDRESS_SPEC() + exec::SIZEOF_FRAME * exec::MAX_FRAME_NUM` (lines 47–51), while `fn from_raw_paddr(paddr: Paddr)` has no `requires` clause and now ensures both `res.paddr() == paddr` and `res.wf()` (lines 134–138).
- **Problem:** For an input at or above the stated bound, the two postconditions imply both that the result's address equals that input and that the same address is below the bound. The contract therefore grants callers a false range fact for an unrestricted input; a verified implementation cannot establish it, while a trusted implementation would turn it into an unsound assumption.
- **Suggestion:** Add the address-bound requirement to `from_raw_paddr` (preferably via a precisely named reusable predicate), and prove it at each call site before constructing the lock. If the runtime constructor intentionally accepts arbitrary raw addresses, remove `res.wf()` and establish `wf()` only after validation.

## Low

None.

## Evidence check record

- Read the authoritative patch in full and compared the changed declarations and their surrounding source in the captured before/after trees.
- Traced all captured `PTL::from_raw_paddr` call sites and checked the definition of the newly added `wf` predicate. The signature itself has no input restriction that could refute the finding.
- Checked the patch for changed `#[verifier::rlimit(...)]` attributes and new or materially changed external specifications for `std`, `core`, or `alloc`; none are present.
- The `path_wf` refactoring was compared with its prior formula. The new adjacent-node `points_to` relation uses `level_at_path_index(j) = j + 1`, matching the former PTE level for adjacent indices, so no contract regression was reported there.
- Per the fast-review constraint, no Verus run, build, history analysis, exhaustive guideline pass, or isolated caller experiment was performed. Findings are based on static source and contract evidence only.

issues.description: The present-entry unmap branch assumes that the current PTE is absent from the SPT and calls `Entry::replace` under the same impossible precondition, even though `is_present` has just established that the PTE is present.
issues.rationale: Control reaches the replacement branch only when `cur_entry.pte.is_present(spt)` returned true. Its trait contract guarantees that a true result implies the SPT PTE map contains the current PTE address. The branch then assumes the negation, and problem-side `Entry::replace` independently requires that negation. # Review: PR 923 snapshot (`before` → `after`)

> Produced from `diff.patch` as the authoritative change, with the supplied `before/` and `after/` trees used only for context.
> Scope: `ostd/src/mm/heap/{mod.rs,slot.rs,slot_list.rs}` and `ostd/src/mm/mod.rs` as changed by `diff.patch`.

**Bottom line:** The verification work for the free-list itself is substantial, but this patch enables `mm::heap` only after commenting out the slab implementation, the global allocator bridge, and large-slot allocation/deallocation. That is a blocking executable/API regression, and the newly specified `push` operation also permits a no-panic path that irreversibly consumes an invalid slot. Restore the executable heap surface before merging, then retain the ghost ownership model around that unchanged runtime code.

## High

### The newly exported heap module removes its allocator implementation and most of its public API

- **Guideline:** `preserve-exec-code`
- **Location:** `ostd/src/mm/heap/mod.rs:3`
- **Evidence:** The patch changes `//pub mod heap;` to `pub mod heap;`, but the enabled module now contains `/*mod slab;*/`, comments out `slab::{Slab, SlabMeta}`, and encloses `GlobalHeapAllocator`, the `#[alloc_error_handler]`, `#[global_allocator] static HEAP_ALLOCATOR`, and the complete `GlobalAlloc for AllocDispatch` implementation in one block comment (`after/ostd/src/mm/heap/mod.rs:3-148`). It also comments out `HeapSlot::alloc_large`, `HeapSlot::dealloc_large`, and `LargeAllocFrameMeta` (`after/ostd/src/mm/heap/slot.rs:141-195,237-241`). The retained proc macro still generates `ostd::mm::heap::GlobalHeapAllocator` references (`after/ostd/libs/ostd-macros/src/lib.rs:144`), but that trait no longer exists in the compiled module.
- **Problem:** This is not a proof-only refactoring: the public module that the patch activates cannot provide the documented slab/global-allocation API, downstream uses of `#[global_heap_allocator]` expand against a missing trait, and the crate no longer registers the allocator dispatch shown by the original executable code. Large-slot construction and release disappear as well.
- **Suggestion:** Restore the original executable definitions and exports unchanged. Add contracts, ghost fields, or narrowly scoped verifier exclusions around unsupported pieces while preserving their Rust behavior; if the allocator/slab code is not ready to be enabled, keep `mm::heap` disabled rather than publishing a deliberately truncated replacement.

## Medium

### `push` can consume a non-slab slot without returning it

- **Guideline:** `api-preconditions`
- **Location:** `ostd/src/mm/heap/slot_list.rs:136`
- **Evidence:** The new precondition is conditional: `cfg!(feature = "allow_panic") ==> slot.slot_info() is SlabSlot` (`after/ostd/src/mm/heap/slot_list.rs:137-145`). In a build without `allow_panic`, the non-slab arm executes `return` (`after/ostd/src/mm/heap/slot_list.rs:160-165`). The function takes `slot: HeapSlot` by value and returns `()`, while its postcondition merely says the list remains unchanged for that arm (`after/ostd/src/mm/heap/slot_list.rs:146-153`). `HeapSlot` owns the exclusive `PointsToRaw` permission introduced at `after/ostd/src/mm/heap/slot.rs:36-37`.
- **Problem:** A legal verified call in the no-panic configuration can pass `SlotInfo::LargeSlot`; the call then consumes the only abstract owner of the memory, inserts nothing, and offers no result through which the caller can recover it. This also conflicts with the rustdoc statement that invalid slot kinds panic.
- **Suggestion:** For the current unit-returning API, require `slot.slot_info() is SlabSlot` unconditionally (and keep the size/alignment obligations under that valid case). If rejecting non-slab slots is intended runtime behavior, change the API to return the rejected `HeapSlot` in an error/result and specify that ownership-preserving outcome.

## Low

| Finding | Guideline | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| The verifier trust boundary on the thread-safety impls is not disclosed (`ostd/src/mm/heap/slot_list.rs:41-53`). | `document-verified-apis` | Both `unsafe impl Sync` and `unsafe impl Send` are newly marked `#[verifier::external]`. The adjacent safety comment argues the Rust aliasing discipline but does not tell reviewers that these unsafe impls are assumed rather than verified. Add one concise trust-boundary statement identifying exactly what remains externally justified. |

## Evidence check record

- Read all 585 lines of `diff.patch`; treated it as the immutable, authoritative review input.

# Review: PR 924 snapshot (`diff.patch`)

> Scope: the 1,012-line authoritative `diff.patch`, covering eight changed paths, checked against the supplied `before/` and `after/` trees. This was a fast isolated review limited to maintainability, proof/trust assumptions, API contracts and invariants, specification reuse, and changed `rlimit` values above 200.

**Bottom line:** The verification conversion weakens several executable tests into proofs that check only cursor/result shape and no longer check the bytes or values named by the tests. Separately, the newly extended fallible `read_val`/`write_val` contracts still do not expose their documented success behavior, which is already visible in the converted caller having to discard both results.

## High

No high-severity findings.

## Medium

### M1 — Preserve the value-level assertions when converting the I/O tests

- **Guideline:** `preserve-exec-code`
- **Location:** `ostd/src/mm/test.rs:37`
- **Evidence:** The converted `read_write_u32_infallible` still says `/// Tests reading and writing u32 values in Infallible mode`, but its final checks are only `assert!(r1.is_ok());` and `assert!(r2.is_ok());` at lines 78 and 82. The before-version checked both the backing bytes (`assert_eq!(&buffer[..4], &val1.to_le_bytes()[..]);`) and the round trip (`assert_eq!(val1, read_val1);`). The same loss recurs in `fill_infallible` (after lines 181–187 omit the former `assert_eq!(buffer, vec![0xFF; 8])`), `skip_read_infallible` (after line 222 checks only `copied == 3`, replacing `assert_eq!(read_buffer, [30, 40, 50])`), and `write_val_infallible` (after lines 398–412 omit the former final buffer assertion).
- **Problem:** These edits do not merely add proof scaffolding: they remove the observations that detect incorrect data movement. The resulting functions can verify even if an operation advances the expected number of bytes while copying or producing the wrong value, so their names and comments overstate what is tested.
- **Suggestion:** Keep the original `#[ktest]` bodies and their value assertions executable, and add separate verified proof clients if the current memory model cannot establish those assertions. If a single converted function must serve both roles, first strengthen the underlying byte/value contracts enough to retain the original assertions; do not delete the assertions to make the proof pass.

### M2 — Specify the successful outcome of fallible value I/O

- **Guideline:** `api-postconditions`
- **Location:** `ostd/src/mm/io.rs:1096` and `ostd/src/mm/io.rs:1862`
- **Evidence:** Both materially changed contracts now pin only the undersized case—`old(self).remain_spec() < core::mem::size_of::<T>() ==> r == Err(Error::InvalidArgs)` for `read_val`, and the analogous `avail_spec()` clause for `write_val`—plus rollback on `Err`. Neither contract has an `Ok` arm. This contradicts the existing `write_val` verified-properties text at lines 1850–1853, which promises, “On success, the cursor advances by `size_of::<T>()`.” The natural converted caller demonstrates the gap: `fallible_read_write` assigns `write_result` and `read_result` at `ostd/src/mm/test.rs:432` and `:444` but cannot assert success, cursor movement, or `read_result == Ok(val)`.

- **Suggestion:** Add conditional `Ok` postconditions that expose the documented cursor advance and unchanged end/range identity. For `read_val`, also relate the returned `T` to the bytes read through the established `Pod`/memory-view model; for `write_val`, relate the successful write to `new_val` where the fallible memory model supports it. Preserve page-fault nondeterminism: this need not claim that a sufficiently large request must succeed.

# Review: PR 927 snapshot `cd548f6f2503`

> Fast, non-exhaustive VOSTD review of the supplied `diff.patch`, using the paired `before/` and `after/` trees for context.
> Scope: maintainability, proof/trust boundaries, assumptions, API contracts and invariants, `rlimit > 200`, and specification reuse. History, Verus runs, exhaustive checklist coverage, and caller experiments were explicitly excluded.

**Bottom line:** The new `Pod` derive is unsound for ordinary `repr(C)` structs because it permits padding while the unsafe trait exposes the entire object representation as initialized bytes. The PR's own `TestPodStruct` demonstrates an accepted padded layout. The derive also emits a trait path that makes direct downstream use of `ostd-pod` depend unexpectedly on an `ostd` crate being present.

## High

### Reject padded layouts before generating the unsafe `Pod` impl

- **Guideline:** `centralize-trusted-boundaries`
- **Location:** `ostd/libs/ostd-pod/derive/src/lib.rs:51`
- **Evidence:** The macro accepts any struct having one of the listed representations and then checks only its fields:

  ```rust
  if !has_valid_repr(attrs) {
      panic!("{} has invalid repr to implement Pod", ident.to_string());
  }
  // ...
  unsafe impl #impl_generics #trait_tokens for #ident #type_generics
      where #(#pod_where_predicates),* {}
  ```

  The unsafe trait contract says that `T: Pod` supports conversion from arbitrary `size_of::<T>()` bytes and implements `as_bytes` by exposing all `size_of::<Self>()` bytes (`ostd/libs/ostd-pod/src/lib.rs:12-23,64-67`). The newly derived test type makes the gap concrete: `TestPodStruct { a: u32, b: u64 }` is declared to have size 16 (`ostd/src/mm/test.rs:32-40`), although its fields contain only 12 bytes, so its accepted `repr(C)` layout contains four padding bytes.
- **Problem:** Constructing this struct normally does not initialize its padding, but the derived `Pod` impl permits safe `as_bytes()` to read that padding through a `&[u8]`. That violates the unsafe trait's arbitrary-bytes promise and can expose uninitialized bytes through a safe API; the same issue applies to padded tuples and unions.
- **Suggestion:** Make the derive reject every layout with padding before emitting the unsafe impl (including generic and union cases), following a proven `Pod` derive design such as compile-time layout assertions. Add compile-fail cases for the demonstrated `u32`/`u64` struct and other internal/trailing-padding layouts; do not use this padded type as a positive test.

## Medium

### Generate a stable trait path for direct `ostd-pod` users

- **Guideline:** `api-preconditions`
- **Location:** `ostd/libs/ostd-pod/derive/src/lib.rs:152`
- **Evidence:** `pod_trait_tokens()` selects `::ostd_pod::Pod` only when `CARGO_PKG_NAME` is exactly `ostd` or `ostd-pod`; every other consuming package receives `::ostd::Pod` (`lib.rs:152-165`). At the same time, `ostd-pod` enables the derive by default and re-exports it (`ostd/libs/ostd-pod/Cargo.toml:17-18`; `ostd/libs/ostd-pod/src/lib.rs:121-122`).
- **Problem:** A downstream crate that directly depends on `ostd-pod` and writes `#[derive(ostd_pod::Pod)]` is made to resolve `::ostd::Pod`, so the advertised derive fails unless that crate also happens to depend on and name `ostd`. The generated API therefore imposes a hidden dependency unrelated to the trait being derived.
- **Suggestion:** Resolve the actual crate exporting the trait (for example with a crate-name resolver supporting dependency renames), or make the derive consistently target `ostd_pod` and arrange the necessary self-alias/re-export behavior. Add an integration fixture whose package name is neither `ostd` nor `ostd-pod` and which depends only on `ostd-pod`.

## Low

| Finding | Guideline | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| Propose the generally reusable `Vec::index_mut` specification upstream | `upstream-reusable-specs` | `verified_libs/vstd_extra/src/external/vec.rs:14-25` adds a project-local `assume_specification` for the standard `alloc::vec::Vec` API, expressed entirely through vstd's generic `SliceIndexSpec`. The supplied change records no upstream plan. Once its contract is validated, propose it to Verus/vstd so other projects can reuse one maintained trust boundary instead of forking the same standard-library model. |

None.

None.

**Rule:** `upstream-reusable-specs`

The patch adds project-local external specifications for the standard-library implementations `<[T] as AsMut<[T]>>::as_mut` and `<Vec<T, A> as IndexMut<I>>::index_mut`. Both contracts describe generic `core`/`alloc` behavior, contain no VOSTD-specific model, and are reusable by any Verus client that mutably reborrows a slice or indexes a `Vec`. The patch contains no recorded plan to propose them to upstream Verus. Keeping these generic models only in `vstd_extra` creates another trusted contract source that can drift from upstream library models.

Propose both specifications upstream (or reference an existing upstream issue/PR in the change). Keep a temporary local copy only while that work is pending, with the upstream tracking reference recorded beside it.

- Checked the `to_flat_binary` precondition, loop invariant, prefix model, overlap behavior, mapping arithmetic, and the only caller. No Verus verification, compilation, tests, isolated caller experiments, network lookups, or repository-history checks were run. Conclusions are from static inspection of the supplied patch, before/after trees, installed `xmas-elf 0.10.0` source, and installed Rust standard-library source. # Review: PR 96 patch snapshot (`diff.patch`)

> Scope: `diff.patch` is the authoritative change set; `before/xtask/src/main.rs` and `after/xtask/src/main.rs` were used only for surrounding context.
>
> No verification was run: fast review mode explicitly excluded Verus, experiments, repository history, and exhaustive guideline checks.

**Bottom line:** The new Verus-root discovery does not establish the directory-layout invariant on which its callers rely. A valid `VERUS_PATH` or `PATH` entry that is a symlink, wrapper, or normally installed binary can therefore be accepted while producing an unrelated directory as the “source root,” breaking documentation and line-count commands. This should be fixed before merge.

## High

None.

## Medium

### The inferred source root is accepted without validating the Verus layout

- **Category:** API contract / path invariant (`api-postconditions`)
- **Location:** `xtask/src/main.rs:682`
- **Evidence:** `get_verus()` explicitly accepts a binary from `VERUS_PATH` or `PATH` (`locate(..., Some("VERUS_PATH"), ...)` at lines 109–116), but `get_verus_root()` merely walks up three parents and accepts the result when `root.is_dir()` (lines 683–690). Callers then assume source-tree-specific children exist, including `root/tools/line_count` (lines 546–550), `root/target/release/verusdoc` (lines 657–674), and `root/target-verus/debug/...` in `exec_doc`.
- **Problem:** Being an existing directory does not prove that the result is the Verus source root. For example, a `verus` symlink in a bin directory is not canonicalized, and an installed `/usr/local/bin/verus` produces `/usr` after three parent traversals; both satisfy `is_dir()` while pointing the subsequent commands at unrelated paths. This contradicts the existing lookup contract that advertises `VERUS_PATH` and `PATH` as supported ways to select the binary.
- **Suggestion:** Resolve symlinks before inference and validate source-root markers/required children rather than only `is_dir()`. If arbitrary installed or wrapped binaries cannot identify their source checkout reliably, add an explicit Verus-source-root override (with a default of `tools/verus/source`) and use it for source-dependent operations; keep binary discovery independent.

## Low

None.

## Evidence check record

- Read all 115 lines of the authoritative `diff.patch`.
- Compared the complete before/after file and inspected every changed caller of `get_verus_root()`, plus the existing `get_verus()` lookup order.
- Static refutation check: the new guard proves only that the third ancestor exists; no suffix check, canonicalization, source marker, or required-child validation establishes the claimed root.
- No `#[verifier::rlimit(...)]` change or new/materially changed `std`, `core`, or `alloc` external specification appears in the patch.
- No proof or trust-boundary code is changed. No API precondition issue was found beyond the postcondition/path-invariant defect above.
- No compilation, Verus verification, repository-history inspection, or isolated caller experiment was performed, per the requested fast-review constraints.

# Review: `diff.patch` (PR 97 fixture `d67afbc9e914`)

> Produced from the supplied before/after snapshots and `diff.patch`, using the VOSTD maintainability, proof-engineering, and API-contract criteria.  
> Scope: fast, non-exhaustive review of `pr-97-d67afbc9e914/diff.patch`; surrounding context was read from the matching `before/` and `after/` files.

**Bottom line:** The new level check changes executable traversal behavior: after descending to a level-1 page table, `take_next` now exits without examining or unmapping the base-page entry and reports the whole requested range as not mapped. This conflicts directly with the function's documented behavior and should block the change. The widened `Entry::replace` contract also still does not expose the documented returned old child, so verified callers cannot reason about the result.

## High

### `take_next` stops before examining level-1 entries

- **Guideline:** `preserve-exec-code`
- **Location:** `lock-protocol/src/mm/page_table/cursor/mod.rs:718`
- **Quoted evidence:** The loop changed from `while self.0.va < end` to `while self.0.va < end && self.0.level > 1`. `push_level` establishes `self.level == old(self).level - 1` (`cursor/mod.rs:327`) and the `PageTableRef` arm calls it (`cursor/mod.rs:755-768`). The loop's fall-through result is `PageTableItem::NotMapped { va: start, len }` (`cursor/mod.rs:864-865`), while the rustdoc promises that the function finds and removes the first mapped page in the following range (`cursor/mod.rs:673-686`).
- **Problem:** When traversal descends from level 2 to level 1, the added guard makes the next loop test fail even though `self.0.va < end`. The level-1 entry is therefore never inspected or replaced, and the function returns `NotMapped` for a range that may contain a mapped base page. This is not a behavior-preserving proof-only edit, and no `Origin Rust:` record or unchanged-behavior demonstration accompanies it.
- **Suggestion:** Restore the executable loop condition `while self.0.va < end`. Carry the fact needed by the body through a suitable invariant or restructure the proof around the level-1 case without excluding that case from runtime traversal; retain an adjacent `Origin Rust:` block only if an executable rewrite is genuinely unavoidable and demonstrate semantic equivalence.

## Medium

### The widened `replace` API does not specify its returned old child

- **Guideline:** `api-postconditions`
- **Location:** `lock-protocol/src/mm/page_table/node/entry.rs:108`
- **Quoted evidence:** The patch removes `!old(spt).ptes@.value().contains_key(self.pte.pte_paddr() as int)` from `replace`'s `requires`, so replacement of a present entry is now admitted. Its documentation says, `The old child is returned.` (`entry.rs:93-95`), but the `ensures` block at lines 113-123 never mentions the named return value `res`; `match new_child { _ => true }` is also tautological.
- **Problem:** The contract change makes the old, present mapping a meaningful caller-visible result, yet no postcondition relates `res` to the pre-state PTE or `old(spt)`. A verified caller can receive the value but cannot establish that it is the child that was replaced, which is the API's stated purpose.
- **Suggestion:** Add a postcondition that characterizes `res` from the pre-state entry/PTE model (and, where useful, characterizes the installed `new_child` in the final state). Express the exact result with `returns` if the existing model provides a type-correct expression; otherwise use a non-tautological `ensures` relation over `res` and `old(spt)`.

## Low

No evidence-backed low-severity findings.

## Evidence check record

- Read the complete supplied `diff.patch` and compared both changed files against their matching `before/` and `after/` snapshots.
- Checked the traversal premise statically: the `PageTableRef` branch calls `push_level`, whose postcondition reduces `level` by one; the added loop guard excludes the resulting level-1 state before `cur_entry` and `replace` execute.
- Checked the `replace` signature and postconditions statically: the removed precondition widens accepted pre-states, while no remaining postcondition references `res` or relates it to the old entry.
- No `#[verifier::rlimit(...)]` change appears in the patch, so the `rlimit > 200` check was not triggered. No new or materially changed `std`/`core`/`alloc` external specification appears, so the upstream-spec-reuse workflow check was not triggered. No new spec/model/lemma was introduced for which a concrete reuse candidate could be established from the supplied scope.
- **No-verification disclosure:** Per the requested fast mode, no Verus run, isolated caller experiment, history inspection, or exhaustive guideline checklist was performed. The findings are based on source-level before/after evidence only.

# Review: PR #99 isolated patch

> Scope: `pr-99-08de0794bf8f/diff.patch` is authoritative; the matching `before/` and `after/` snapshots were used only for surrounding context and line locations.

**Bottom line:** The patch makes `PageTableGuard` the concrete guard used by cursor and entry code, but its trusted constructor promises validity for arbitrary raw inputs, and its production PTE update path assumes the key memory-model and preservation facts it advertises. Both defects let downstream proofs consume page-table validity without establishing it, so this patch should not merge until those trust gaps are removed or moved to a narrow, justified boundary.

## High

### `from_raw_paddr` fabricates a well-formed guard from unrestricted inputs

- **Guidelines:** `complete-external-contracts`, `centralize-trusted-boundaries`, `api-preconditions`
- **Location:** `lock-protocol/src/mm/page_table/node/mod.rs:113`
- **Evidence:** `PageTableGuard::wf` requires both `pa_is_valid_pt_address(self.paddr as int)` and `level_is_in_range(self.level as int)` (lines 54–57), where `level_is_in_range` is `1 <= level <= MAX_NR_LEVELS` and a valid page-table address must be a valid kernel address aligned to `SIZEOF_FRAME`. Nevertheless, the new trusted function has no preconditions and states:

  ```rust
  #[verifier::external_body]
  pub fn from_raw_paddr(paddr: Paddr, level: PagingLevel) -> (res: Self)
      ensures
          res.wf(),
          res.paddr_spec() == paddr,
          res.level_spec() == level,
  ```

  Thus calls such as a level of `0` simultaneously yield `res.level_spec() == 0` and `res.wf()`, whose second conjunct says that level is in the range starting at `1`. The old trait constructor only related the returned address to its input; this patch newly strengthens the concrete trusted boundary to assert full validity.
- **Problem:** The contract is false for legal Rust inputs and can inject contradictory facts into every cursor path that reconstructs a guard from a PTE address. `external_body` hides rather than discharges the missing validity obligations.
- **Suggestion:** Require `pa_is_valid_pt_address(paddr as int)` and `level_is_in_range(level as int)` at this boundary, prove those facts at each caller before reconstruction, and remove `external_body` if the struct literal then verifies. If raw reconstruction genuinely depends on a lock/ownership protocol, encode that protocol token in the constructor instead of promising `wf()` from integers alone.

### The concrete PTE mutation path assumes its advertised invariants

- **Guidelines:** `centralize-trusted-boundaries`, `complete-external-contracts`
- **Locations:** `lock-protocol/src/mm/page_table/node/mod.rs:149`; `lock-protocol/src/mm/page_table/node/entry.rs:94`
- **Evidence:** The new concrete `PageTableGuard::write_pte` promises `spt.wf()`, allocator invariants, stable instance IDs, and `frame_keys_do_not_change`, but its body assumes the facts needed to access and preserve the model:

  ```rust
  assume(spt.perms@[frame_idx].1@.mem_contents().is_init());
  ...
  assume(points_to.pptr() == p);
  ...
  assume(idx < frame.ptes.len());
  ...
  assume(spt.wf());  // TODO: P0
  assume(spec_helpers::frame_keys_do_not_change(spt, old(spt)));  // TODO: P0
  ```

  Its caller `Entry::replace` likewise introduces the missing ownership relationship locally:

  ```rust
  assume(spt.perms@.contains_key(exec::frame_addr_to_index_spec(self.node.paddr())));
  // FIXME: Add this to entry well-formedness
  ```

  These assumptions previously lived in the deleted `FakePageTableLock` under `exec/mod.rs`; the patch moves them into the concrete `PageTableGuard` now used by normal cursor and entry APIs.
- **Problem:** Verification of every replacement can now rely on post-state well-formedness and frame preservation even though the implementation explicitly does not prove them. This is a material expansion of the production trust surface, not merely unfinished proof cleanup, and it can conceal a mismatch between `spt.perms`, the pointed-to frame, and `spt.frames`—the body itself calls out that inconsistency as `TODO: P0`.
- **Suggestion:** Make the guard/entry invariant carry the permission-map membership, initialization, pointer identity, and PTE-length facts; require that invariant at the mutation boundary; then prove post-state `spt.wf()` and frame-key preservation from the actual remove/write/reinsert transition. Until that proof exists, keep this implementation out of the verified production guard rather than importing the fake implementation's assumptions.

## Medium

No evidence-backed medium-severity findings.

## Low

No useful low-severity findings.

## Evidence check record

- Read all 808 lines of `diff.patch` and inspected the complete changed `before/` and `after/` files for line-level context.
- Rechecked the new `wf`, `from_raw_paddr`, `write_pte`, and `Entry::replace` contracts and bodies against their direct callers in the captured snapshots. The unrestricted constructor contract directly conflicts with the definition of `wf`; the mutation finding is supported by explicit `assume` statements and the in-source `TODO: P0`/`FIXME` markers.
- No `#[verifier::rlimit(...)]` change appears in the patch, so the `> 200` workflow check did not trigger. No new or materially changed external specification for a `std`, `core`, or `alloc` API appears in scope.
- No separate spec-reuse finding was retained: the changed address/level predicates reuse existing `sub_page_table` helpers rather than introducing competing definitions.
- **Verification disclosure:** Per the fast-review override, no Git history, repository-wide guideline enumeration, Verus run, test, CI run, caller experiment, or exhaustive rule audit was performed. Findings are based solely on static inspection of the authoritative patch and its captured before/after context.

issues.description: SubPageTable initialization creates a root frame but leaves its executable permission resource absent and relies on an invariant that inconsistently treats the same key as both a frame index and a physical address.
issues.rationale: The initialized state-machine frames map contains the root at p.addr(), but the executable SubPageTable uses HashMap::new() for perms. Its written invariant requires every frame key to have a permission entry, while also interpreting the quantified key as an index in PHYSICAL_BASE + i * SIZEOF_FRAME and frame_index_to_addr(i), so the empty and mis-keyed representation cannot establish wf without the explicit assume. Repair bc92f16a consistently uses physical-address keys, inserts p.addr() -> (p, Tracked(pt)), and changes assume(wf) to assert(wf). The allocator postcondition supplies the normalized address-validity fact needed by this same repair; it is not an independent defect.
